headline: JMAP answers with the error types, limits and thread boundaries its RFCs define
summary: A JMAP refusal now carries one of the four request-level problem types RFC 8620 §3.6.1 defines, `unknownCapability`, `notJSON`, `notRequest` or `limit` with a member naming the cap, sent as `application/problem+json` with `status` and `detail`; the listener had been sending its own codes, and the HTTP and WebSocket transports answered the same input differently. A method error is the bare name §3.6.2 prints rather than a URI, so a client matching `unknownMethod` or any RFC 8621 set error matches. `maxObjectsInGet` and `maxObjectsInSet` were defined in every profile and read by nothing: an `Email/get` handler received 250,000 ids under a profile whose limit is 500, and a `/get` or `/set` over the cap is now `requestTooLarge` before the handler runs, counted after result references resolve. A request body is parsed with the profile's `maxSizeRequest` rather than a 1 MiB default, so a valid 1.17 MB request is no longer reported as invalid JSON. The session's `urn:ietf:params:jmap:core` capability was an empty object and now carries the eight properties RFC 8620 §2 requires, built from the limits the listener applies. `b.mailStore` threaded messages across every folder in the store, so an account holder who appended a message naming a Message-ID could tell whether any other account on the server held it, and a message delivered to two accounts split the second account's thread; a folder now carries an owner and a thread stays inside it. A result reference path with `*` applies the rest of the pointer to every item and flattens the results, an account-scoped method without an `accountId` is refused before its handler runs, and `EmailSubmission/set` compares the envelope sender against the identity by address rather than by exact string.

items.title: A message sent with the null reverse path gets no DSN, in either spelling
items.body: The guard that stops a DSN being generated for the null reverse path compared `envelope.from` with `""` exactly. On the wire the null reverse path is written `<>`, and that is the spelling it arrives in, so a caller passing it through got a DSN for a message RFC 5321 §4.5.5 says must not receive one: a DSN's `To:` is the original `from`, so bouncing a bounce addresses it to nobody and, to a less careful peer, to itself. The question is now a predicate that recognizes both spellings, so a second site added later cannot repeat the omission. The MX listener already normalized the wire form, which is why this was latent rather than live.

items.title: A forged Authentication-Results is stripped in every spelling the readers accept
items.body: `b.mail.server.mx` removed a peer's forged `Authentication-Results` by matching the field name as a literal line prefix and reading the authserv-id off that same line, while every reader downstream is an RFC 5322 parser. Three spellings the parser accepts as the same header went straight through: folded before the authserv-id (RFC 5322 §2.2.3), a quoted authserv-id (RFC 8601 §2.2), and whitespace before the colon (RFC 5322 §4.5.8 obs-optional). Measured on a real session: a peer failing SPF and DMARC delivered a folded forged header claiming `dmarc=pass`, and the stored message carried two verdicts under the receiving server's own name. The strip now unfolds the header block and reads the field name and authserv-id under the same grammar the parsers use, including a quoted id and leading comments. `b.mail.server.mx.stripForgedAuthResults(message, authservId)` is exported.

items.title: SPF reads its version tag the way its ABNF writes it
items.body: SPF record selection compared the version case-sensitively, so `V=spf1 -all` was not seen as an SPF record at all and a domain publishing a strict policy evaluated as if it published nothing. RFC 7208 §12 writes the version as the quoted ABNF literal `"v=spf1"`, and RFC 5234 §2.3 makes quoted literals case-insensitive, so both halves fold. The other record types do not fold the same way and a uniform rule would be wrong in the other direction: DMARC, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT spell their version value in hex, which is exact, and TLS-RPT spells even the tag name in hex. `b.structuredFields.recordVersionMatches` takes `valueIgnoresCase` for the one grammar that needs it, and MTA-STS no longer shares a constant with TLS-RPT, whose name case differs from its own.

items.title: Authentication-Results reports the dmarc header.from as a domain
items.body: The header this framework writes carried `header.from=someone@example.com`, where the IANA Email Authentication Methods registry defines that property as the domain of the `From` field, which is also the only part DMARC evaluates (RFC 7489 §3.1). A consumer reading the property as specified and calling `parseDomain` on it got a refusal, correctly, and every aggregate report that arrived was recorded with an unreadable carrier domain and left out of the reading a policy decision rested on. Nothing failed loudly. The domain is emitted, and `b.mail.authResults.emit` refuses an address under a domain-valued property rather than publishing the author's local part in a header every intermediary reads. `smtp.mailfrom` is unchanged: RFC 8601 §2.7.1 defines it as the envelope address.

items.title: A message's shape can be read without decoding its content
items.body: `b.safeMime.parse` decoded every body on every call, so a consumer that wanted only the shape of a message, whether it carries a file and how many, had to decode all of its content to find out. Measured against a real store at a page size of 50: the listing alone 153 ms, reading the octets 1385 ms, and reading plus parsing 7526 ms for 2 MB messages, of which about 6100 ms is the decoding. `parse(bytes, { structureOnly: true })` walks the tree and leaves each leaf's `body` null with its `encodedSize` reported, under every cap and allowlist the ordinary mode applies. Reading the octets alone still costs about 5.5 ms per message whatever its size, so that mode does not by itself make per-render derivation viable, which is why the answer is now stored: `b.mailStore` records `has_attachment` and `attachment_count` from the parse it already does at append and carries them in the fetch and listing projections as `hasAttachment` and `attachmentCount`.

items.title: b.mailStore threads inside one account, so a Message-ID in another account is not observable
items.body: `appendMessage` looked each `In-Reply-To` and `References` message id up in `message_id_hash` across the whole messages table, with no folder condition and no ordering, and took the first matching row's thread root; `threadFor` then returned every row with that root, in every folder. One `b.mail.server.jmap` listener takes one store for every account `accountsFor` returns. An account holder who appended a message naming some Message-ID, by IMAP APPEND or by mailing themself, got their own objectid as the thread root only when no message anywhere in the store carried that id, and another account's objectid otherwise, which a JMAP `Email/get` reporting `threadId` shows them: any account holder could test whether another account held any Message-ID they chose. Separately, a message delivered to two accounts put a later reply in the first account's thread and left the second account's own copy in a thread alone. `createFolder(name, { owner })` records the account that holds a folder, `appendMessage(folder, bytes, { threadScope })` names the scope directly, and every message carries the resulting scope. The Message-ID lookup and `threadFor` match only rows in that scope, and the lookup orders by `received_at` then `objectid` so the root does not depend on row order. Folders that declare no owner share the scope `""`, so a single-account store is unchanged.

items.title: A refused IMAP or ManageSieve literal no longer leaves its payload to be parsed as commands
items.body: `b.mail.server.imap` read a command line, handed it to `b.guardImapCommand`, and on a refusal wrote `BAD` and returned without arming the literal reader, so the octets the client had announced arrived as ordinary lines and were executed as commands. RFC 7888 makes this reachable with no cooperation from the server: a non-synchronizing `{N+}` literal needs no continuation, so the payload is already in flight when the refusal is written. Measured: `a1 LOGIN {7+}` followed by `z9 NOOP` answered the refusal and then `z9 OK NOOP completed`. Bytes the sender presented as data became protocol. The same shape was live in `b.mail.server.managesieve`, where an unauthenticated `PUTSCRIPT "x" {11+}` was refused with `NO "AUTHENTICATE first"` and its announced script then ran as a command. Both listeners now consume and discard exactly the announced octets before the next line is parsed, bounded by the profile's literal cap, the body-rate window and the literal deadline; anything beyond the announced count is charged as ordinary pipelined data. An IMAP literal larger than the cap closes the connection instead, since a byte stream that cannot be located again is not recoverable. A synchronizing `{N}` is untouched: its client waits for a continuation the refusal never sends, so nothing is in flight and consuming would eat the client's next command. `b.guardImapCommand.announcedLiteral(line)` reads the announced size and form.

items.title: An account-scoped JMAP method is refused when no account is named
items.body: The account check compared every `*accountId` argument against the accounts `accountsFor` returns and skipped an argument that was absent or null, so `Email/get` and every other method RFC 8620 §1.6.2 gives a mandatory `accountId` ran its handler with no account named. Such a call is now `invalidArguments` before the handler runs. `b.mail.serverRegistry.jmapMethodTakesAccount(name)` answers which methods take one; `Core/echo` is the one that does not.

items.title: EmailSubmission/set compares the envelope sender with the identity by address
items.body: `envelope.mailFrom` was compared with the identity's address as an exact string, so a sender whose domain differed only in case, or gave an internationalized domain in its A-label form, was refused, while an identity carrying no address accepted any sender. The comparison now folds the domain's case and its A-label form, per RFC 5321 §2.4, folds a subaddress when a delimiter is configured, reads `*@domain` as RFC 8621 §6 defines it, and refuses an identity with no address. The local part keeps its case, which RFC 5321 §2.4 leaves to the receiving host. The `From` header is checked against the identity as well, and a message whose `From` it does not cover is `forbiddenFrom`.

items.title: A refused JMAP request carries an RFC 8620 §3.6.1 problem type
items.body: The listener answered a malformed request with its own codes, `guard-jmap/bad-json`, `guard-jmap/bad-input`, `invalidArguments`, `requestTooLarge` and `limit/<name>`, and put an empty `methodResponses` array and a `sessionState` in the body. A conforming client could not tell a body that would not parse from one that was not a Request, or either from an over-limit request, and the HTTP path sent a different type than the WebSocket path for the same input. A refusal is now `unknownCapability`, `notJSON`, `notRequest`, or `limit` with a `limit` member naming the cap reached (`maxSizeRequest`, `maxCallsInRequest`, `maxUsingCapabilities`, `maxBackRefDepth`), sent as `application/problem+json` with `status` and `detail` and no method-response envelope. Both transports send the same type for the same input. An account backend that fails answers 500 rather than 400.

items.title: A JMAP method error is the bare name RFC 8620 §3.6.2 defines
items.body: A method error was written as the request-level URI, `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:unknownMethod`, where §3.6.2 writes `[ "error", { "type": "unknownMethod" }, "c0" ]`. A client matching the names the RFC prints, and the names RFC 8621 defines for the Email and Mailbox set errors, matched none of them. Method errors are now bare names, and a handler that returns or throws one has that name sent to the client rather than `serverFail`. A returned result counts as an error only when it carries an error name and nothing besides `description` and `properties`, so a result whose own data happens to include a `type` is still a result.

items.title: maxObjectsInGet and maxObjectsInSet are applied
items.body: Both were defined in every `b.guardJmap` profile and documented as enforced, and no code read either: under the strict profile, whose limit is 500, an `Email/get` handler received 250,000 ids and an `Email/set` handler 250,000 destroy ids in one request. A `/get` call's `ids`, and the combined `create`, `update` and `destroy` of a `/set` or `/copy` call, are now counted after result references resolve, and an over-cap call is `requestTooLarge` before the handler runs, per RFC 8620 §5.1 and §5.3. `b.guardJmap.limitsFor(opts)` resolves the caps a profile and posture select.

items.title: A request body is parsed against the declared maxSizeRequest
items.body: A string or Buffer body was measured against the profile's `maxSizeRequest`, 10 MiB under the strict profile, and then parsed with the 1 MiB default of `b.safeJson.parse`, so a valid 1.17 MB request came back as "body is not valid JSON". The parse now uses the profile's limit, and a body over it is the `limit` problem naming `maxSizeRequest`.

items.title: The session publishes the core capability RFC 8620 §2 requires
items.body: `urn:ietf:params:jmap:core` was an empty object, so a client could read none of the limits it has to obey. It now carries `maxSizeUpload`, `maxConcurrentUpload`, `maxSizeRequest`, `maxConcurrentRequests`, `maxCallsInRequest`, `maxObjectsInGet`, `maxObjectsInSet` and `collationAlgorithms`, built from the profile the listener enforces and from `maxBlobBytes`. `create` refuses a `serverCapabilities` core value that differs from what the listener applies.

items.title: A download's Content-Disposition filename survives the round trip
items.body: `b.staticServe` built the `filename*` ext-value with `encodeURIComponent`, whose escaping set is not RFC 8187 §3.2.1 `attr-char`: it emits `'`, `(`, `)` and `*` raw, and the apostrophe is the delimiter the ext-value is parsed on. A file named `reçu café's.pdf` went out as `filename*=UTF-8''re%C3%A7u%20caf%C3%A9's.pdf`, and this framework's own `b.safeMime` reader split on the third delimiter and returned `reçu café`. The encoder now percent-escapes everything outside `attr-char`. Two defects on the reading side went with it: `b.safeMime` took whichever of `filename` and `filename*` appeared first, and RFC 6266 §4.3 writes the plain one first, so the extended name was discarded for every sender that follows the RFC; and an unescaped apostrophe in the value truncated the name rather than being kept. The builder is exported as `b.staticServe.attachmentDisposition(filename)`, because a consumer serving a stranger-named file had to write the header itself, and the obvious way to write it is the way this module wrote it.

items.title: A JMAP Email/get can answer the body-part properties RFC 8621 defines
items.body: `b.mail.server.jmap` carried no `bodyStructure`, `attachments` or `hasAttachment` anywhere, so a JMAP client could not see that a message held a file, list its parts, or fetch one. Nothing was refused and nothing was logged: the response was well formed, the client read the properties it knew, and a message with three files looked the same as one with none. `Email/get` is an operator-supplied handler, so the new piece is the builder it composes: `b.mail.server.jmap.emailBodyProperties(tree, { blobIdPrefix })` turns the tree `b.safeMime.parse` returns into `{ bodyStructure, textBody, htmlBody, attachments, hasAttachment }`, with the `partId` and `blobId` RFC 8621 §4.1.4 puts on each `EmailBodyPart`. A `blobId` is the prefix and the part's path, and the prefix must satisfy the RFC 8620 §1.2 Id grammar, because the download handler in the same module refuses anything else.

items.title: An extracted attachment says which part it came from
items.body: `b.safeMime.extractAttachments` returned `filename`, `contentType`, `body` and `headers` with nothing identifying the part, so a consumer serving one part at a URL had no stable key and paired a second `walk` to this list by index, which is correct only while both traversals visit leaves in the same order. `walk` already computes the position and hands it to its visitor; each entry now carries it as `path`, the index array from the root. `b.safeMime.filenameFromHeaders(headers)` is exported so a caller walking the tree reads filenames the way this module does instead of writing another `Content-Disposition` reader.

items.title: b.mail.dkim.create refuses a private key whose type its algorithm does not name
items.body: `create` parsed `opts.privateKey` and never compared its type with `opts.algorithm`, and nothing downstream compared them either. An RSA key in the `ed25519-sha256` slot produced a `DKIM-Signature` whose `a=` tag said `ed25519-sha256` over an RSA signature: every conforming verifier refuses that message, and the sender saw nothing wrong because the signer returned a header and the send succeeded. An Ed25519 key in the `rsa-sha256` slot failed later and uncoded, throwing Node's `ERR_CRYPTO_UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION` from inside `sign()`. `create` now refuses the mismatch with `dkim/key-algorithm-mismatch`, pairing `rsa-sha256` with an RSA key and `ed25519-sha256` with an Ed25519 key per RFC 6376 §3.3.3 and RFC 8463 §3. `verify` already made this comparison on the receiving side.

items.title: mtaSts.fetch takes an httpClient, as its sibling already did
items.body: `b.network.smtp.policy.mtaSts.fetch` built its HTTPS client inline, so nothing depending on a fetched MTA-STS policy document could be exercised without a live network. `tlsRpt.submit`, in the same module, already declared `httpClient` and read `opts.httpClient || httpClient()`: one question answered two ways. The fetch takes the same option, and its option list is declared, so a misspelled one is refused by name rather than ignored. The policy document decides whether mail to a domain goes out under an enforced TLS policy, which is exactly the path a consumer needs to be able to cover.

items.title: The MTA-STS lookup goes through the resolver the sender pinned
items.body: `b.mail.send.deliver` used `opts.resolver` for the MX and DANE TLSA lookups and called `mtaSts.fetch(domain)` with the domain alone, so `_mta-sts.<domain>` was answered by whatever the host resolves with. That record is the whole decision: RFC 8461 §3.1 gives a receiver one TXT record to declare a policy and a sender that sees none enforces nothing, so a suppressed answer and an honest absence are the same answer. The lookup deciding whether a message goes out under an enforced TLS policy was the one lookup a pinned resolver did not reach. `mtaSts.fetch` and `tlsRpt.fetchPolicy` now take a `resolver` handle alongside the existing `dnsLookup` function, and the composer passes its own through.

items.title: b.guardImapCommand applies the mailbox, sequence-set and SEARCH-depth caps it declares
items.body: Every profile declared `maxMailboxBytes`, `maxSequenceSetItems` and `maxSearchDepth`, the documentation said they were enforced, and no code read any of them: a consumer selecting the strict profile for its sequence-set bound got the line bound instead, so the effective limit moved with the length of the line rather than with the element count the cap names, and nothing bounded SEARCH nesting at all. `validate` now bounds the mailbox-name argument in bytes (`guard-imap-command/mailbox-too-long`), the elements a sequence set expands to, counting a range by its span (`guard-imap-command/sequence-set-too-large`), and the nesting of a SEARCH key outside quoted strings (`guard-imap-command/search-too-deep`). A `UID` prefix is unwrapped so the caps apply to the command it qualifies. A seventh value, `allowLegacyMUtf7`, was declared `true` for the balanced profile while `b.mail.server.imap` derived its own answer from `profile === "permissive"` and refused it: the table now states what the listener has always applied, and the listener reads it through the new `b.mail.server.imap.legacyMUtf7Allowed(profile)` rather than deriving a second answer. `b.guardImapCommand.limitsFor(opts)` resolves the caps a profile and posture select.

items.title: A compliance posture the guard does not know is refused by name
items.body: `b.gateContract.makeProfileResolver` and `b.gateContract.resolveProfileName` dropped a `posture` value their table did not hold and fell through to `profile` or the default, and the 24 guards built on them inherited that. An operator who wrote `{ profile: "permissive", posture: "hippa" }`, or `"HIPAA"` in the wrong case, ran permissive with no signal that the posture had been ignored. Both resolvers now throw `<guard>/bad-posture` naming the value and the postures the guard accepts. `b.guardJmap`, `b.guardImapCommand`, `b.guardPop3Command` and `b.guardManageSieveCommand` each resolved the profile and posture with their own copy of the same code and kept dropping it; all four now use the shared resolver. A posture that is absent, null or empty is not a value and is not refused.

items.title: A guard profile cannot be edited from outside the guard
items.body: `b.guardJmap.limitsFor` returned the profile object itself, so `limitsFor({}).maxCallsInRequest = 9999` raised the cap the guard enforces for every listener in the process. The profiles are frozen.

items.title: The JMAP WebSocket transport applies the request size the session declares
items.body: The WebSocket path carried its own 10 MiB limit in the upgrade cap, the frame-length check and the parse, while the session publishes the profile's `maxSizeRequest`. Under the balanced profile a client was told 50 MiB and refused at 10 MiB. All three read the profile's limit, and `webSocketMaxMessageBytes` overrides it.

items.title: A mail-store move between accounts is refused
items.body: A move kept the message's thread scope, so a message moved from one account's folder into another's sat in the second account's mailbox carrying the first account's thread, and `threadFor` on it listed the first account's messages. A move between folders with different owners throws `mail-store/cross-account-move`; RFC 8621 §5.4 gives `Email/copy` as the cross-account move, and it makes a new Email id.

items.title: A result reference path applies the whole pointer
items.body: `*` returned the array itself and dropped the tokens after it, so the chain RFC 8620 §3.7 uses as its example, `Email/query` to `Email/get` to `Thread/get` to `Email/get` through `/list/*/threadId` and `/list/*/emailIds`, passed the previous method's objects instead of thread ids and message ids. `*` now applies the rest of the pointer to every item and flattens array results into one array. A path no item satisfies fails the call with `invalidResultReference` rather than resolving to the array, an array index follows the RFC 6901 grammar, and an arguments object carrying both `ids` and `#ids` is `invalidArguments`.

items.title: New options
items.body: `b.mail.server.jmap.create` takes `maxConcurrentUpload`, `maxConcurrentRequests` and `collationAlgorithms`, all published in the session. `b.mailStore.createFolder` takes `owner`, and `b.mailStore.appendMessage` takes `threadScope`. `b.guardJmap.limitsFor(opts)` is new.

items.title: A client that matched the old JMAP error strings
items.body: A client matching `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:unknownMethod` and the other method-level URIs should match the bare names instead. A client matching `guard-jmap/bad-json`, `guard-jmap/bad-input` or `urn:ietf:params:jmap:error:requestTooLarge` on a refused request should match `notJSON`, `notRequest` and `limit`. A refused request no longer carries `methodResponses` or `sessionState`.

items.title: A misspelled compliance posture now throws at config time
items.body: A guard call that passes a `posture` outside its table throws `<guard>/bad-posture` where it used to run the default profile silently. If a deployment has been passing one, the message names the value and the postures that guard accepts: `hipaa`, `pci-dss`, `gdpr`, `soc2`. Passing no posture is unchanged.

items.title: A mail store that holds more than one account
items.body: Give each folder an `owner` at `createFolder`, or pass `appendOpts.threadScope` on append. Messages written before this carry the scope `""` and keep their existing thread roots; RFC 8621 §3 makes `threadId` immutable, so moving them into per-account scopes means reinserting them with new objectids.
